correctness.rationale: Reconstructed all definitions and quantifiers: strictly decreasing positive null sequence, arbitrary nonzero real Banach target, every point of its compact domain, norm not necessarily attained at an adjacent pair. The adjacent-slope operator is an onto linear isometry because all quotients are positive weighted averages and the differences telescope. Vanishing adjacent ratios transfer nearly maximal adjacent slopes to base-zero slopes with error at most twice the ratio. On failure, the sparse selected indices have ratio >=delta and mutually separated radii; the ell-infinity coding preserves its norm exactly and its base-zero quotients have gap >=delta/2. At each isolated point all finite quotients are strictly subnorm and their only accumulation limit is also subnorm. No finite sample is used to prove infinite claims.

originality.rationale: The 2023 primary full text supplies only a particular rapidly lacunary compact example; the 2024 work supplies non-strong-attainment on arbitrary metrics and non-pointwise attainment on the full real line. Neither implies a necessary-and-sufficient adjacent-ratio criterion on every monotone convergent sequence, or a closed isometric ell-infinity complement on every failure case. Actual targeted published-results and conventional literature searches did not identify an equivalent or dominating statement. Residual risk from terminology differences and later journal revision remains.

value.rationale: The paper motivates the natural but previously example-based question of when all functions attain the weaker pointwise norm. The result gives an exact iff geometric classification for the entire one-accumulation-point compact metric sequence family. In the failure case it supplies an isometric closed ell-infinity of nonattainers for every nonzero Banach range, strictly stronger than a single counterexample and different from general non-strong-attainment spaceability. The precise adjacent-ratio threshold distinguishes geometrically close compact sets such as {2^(-n^2)} and {2^(-n)}.
